A case constructed for teaching: the underlying CT is real (public archive) and without perforation; free air, bubbles, fat stranding and fluid were added by computer while preserving the image noise. The small mass of the left kidney, by contrast, is real.
In the supine patient, free air rises to the highest parts of the abdomen: under the anterior wall, in front of the liver and along the falciform ligament (which becomes visible because it is surrounded by air). It must be sought with the lung window or a wide window: with the abdominal window small amounts easily escape.
To find the site: extraluminal bubbles concentrated near a viscus, fat stranding, wall thickening, fluid and any leakage of oral contrast indicate the point of perforation. Abundant free air in the epigastrium with bubbles near the antrum or bulb suggests a perforated peptic ulcer (stomach and duodenum contain a lot of air); little air with bubbles in the pelvis suggests the colon (diverticulitis).
Pitfalls: pseudopneumoperitoneum (Chilaiditi, air between skin folds, air in the wall); normal air after surgery (usually disappears in a few days); the absence of oral contrast leakage does not exclude perforation.
Communication: perforation of a hollow viscus is a critical finding to be communicated immediately by voice to the physician who requested the exam and to the surgeon.
Addome acuto: guarda sempre con la fines: Acute abdomen: always look with the lung window under the anterior wall and in front of the liver; if there is free air, look for where bubbles and stranding concentrate.
